summary: Defines the SDP media-level attribute "rtcp-mux-only", which an endpoint uses to signal that it supports only RTP and RTCP multiplexing on a single port. It also updates RFC 5761 by clarifying how an offerer can indicate this. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some programs only know how to share one road for two kinds of traffic. This document adds a short sign that says "I only use the shared road" so the other side does not offer two.

questions: how to indicate exclusive rtcp multiplexing in sdp
can an sdp answer contain rtcp-mux-only
subtitle: A one-word SDP attribute that says an endpoint will only send RTP and RTCP together on a single port.

tldr.problem: RFC 5761 lets endpoints share one port for RTP and RTCP, but if the peer does not agree, both sides fall back to separate ports. Some endpoints cannot do that fallback and had no standard way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8858 defines the media-level SDP attribute 'rtcp-mux-only'. An offerer adds it, together with 'rtcp-mux', to say that multiplexing is the only option; the answerer either accepts with 'rtcp-mux' or rejects the media.
tldr.outcome: Offers can now state that there is no fallback to separate RTCP ports, and RFC 5761 is updated to say the offerer must then disable the media if the answer does not agree.

today: RFC 8858 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted, and it updates RFC 5761.

sections.title: Why Say 'Multiplexing Only'
sections.content:
RFC 5761 defines how to carry RTP (media) and RTCP (control reports) on a single IP address and port, called RTP/RTCP multiplexing. It also defines the SDP attribute rtcp-mux for offering and negotiating it. If the peer does not support multiplexing, both sides are expected to fall back to separate ports for RTP and RTCP.

Some newer applications do not want that fallback. The RFC gives W3C WebRTC applications as an example, since they are not required to interoperate with non-WebRTC clients. Other reasons come from the network: an endpoint on a radio interface may want different bearers for RTP and RTCP, and a gateway to a network where multiplexing cannot be used would otherwise have to demultiplex RTP and RTCP itself.

The RFC warns that using the new attribute in offers may harm interoperability for any entity that ever has to talk to peers that cannot multiplex.
sections.plainLanguage: Most programs can use one shared road or two separate roads. A few can only use the shared one, and this document gives them a way to say so up front.

sections.title: The rtcp-mux-only Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute is named rtcp-mux-only. It has no value, is used at the media level (on an m= line's description), and is not charset dependent. An example is a=rtcp-mux-only.

In an offer, it indicates exclusive support of RTP/RTCP multiplexing for the RTP-based media of that media description. It is defined only for RTP-based media. Using it in an SDP answer is forbidden; in an answer, the plain rtcp-mux attribute says the answerer supports and accepts multiplexing.

Its mux category (from RFC 8859) is IDENTICAL. Inside a BUNDLE group, it must therefore appear on all the multiplexed RTP-based media descriptions. It applies to the whole media description, and it MUST NOT be defined per source with the SDP ssrc attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny label with no extra words. An offer can carry it; an answer must never carry it.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Procedures
sections.content:
Initial offer. To indicate exclusive multiplexing, the offerer MUST add rtcp-mux-only to the media description, and MUST also add rtcp-mux to the same description. If it also uses the SDP rtcp attribute, the address and port in it MUST match the ones used for RTP. Using rtcp is not mandated.

Answer. If the answerer accepts multiplexing, it MUST add rtcp-mux. If it does not, it MUST either reject that media description by setting its port to zero or reject the whole offer. The answerer MUST NOT add rtcp-mux-only.

Offerer processing. If the answer has rtcp-mux, the offerer applies the multiplexing procedures of RFC 5761. If not, it MUST either disable the media (for example with a new offer that has a zero port) or send a new offer without rtcp-mux-only.

Later offers. If exclusive multiplexing was already negotiated, the offerer SHOULD keep rtcp-mux-only (with rtcp-mux). Leaving the attributes out means the offerer no longer wants multiplexing and MUST fall back to separate ports once the offer is accepted. If it was not negotiated before, the offerer MAY now offer it. Switching back and forth is RECOMMENDED against unless a use case demands it.
sections.plainLanguage: The asker shows the sign and the shared-road label. The other side either agrees by showing the shared-road label, or says no. If it says no, the asker has to give up on that stream or ask again without the sign.

sections.title: Update to RFC 5761
sections.content:
This RFC changes two paragraphs of RFC 5761, using OLD and NEW text.

In Section 5.1.1, if the answer has no a=rtcp-mux, the offerer still MUST NOT multiplex and should use separate RTCP ports. The new text adds: if the offerer had indicated in its offer that it cannot send and receive RTCP on a separate port, the offerer MUST disable the media streams associated with the attribute. How that indication is made is outside the scope of RFC 5761 itself. The text also changes the spelling 'signalled' to 'signaled'. The RFC notes that RFC 8035 also updates this section and moves the paragraph, but does not change it.

In Section 5.1.3, when ICE and multiplexing are both wanted, the offer normally carries candidates for both RTP and RTCP plus an a=rtcp: fallback port. The new text adds that an offerer which cannot use a separate RTCP port MUST NOT include RTCP candidates and MUST NOT give a fallback port in a=rtcp:.
sections.plainLanguage: The older rulebook said what to do when the other side says no. This document adds a rule for people who cannot use the backup plan: stop the stream, and do not offer backup roads.

sections.title: ICE Considerations
sections.content:
Under ICE (RFC 8445), an entity that knows the remote peer supports and is willing to use RTP/RTCP multiplexing provides only RTP candidates (component ID 1).

Offering only RTP candidates does not by itself mean exclusive multiplexing, because RTCP candidates are also left out when RTCP is not supported at all. Extra information is therefore needed, and the rtcp-mux-only attribute is that mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Leaving out the second road on the map could mean 'I only use one road' or 'I do not send reports at all'. The sign removes the doubt.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registration
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 3605 and RFC 5761.

IANA registers rtcp-mux-only in the 'Session Description Protocol Parameters' registry as a media-level attribute, not subject to charset, with the purpose 'Indicate exclusive support of RTP/RTCP multiplexing', appropriate values N/A and mux category IDENTICAL.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding the sign creates no new danger beyond the ones that already existed. It was also written down in the official list of labels.

messages.label: Offer
messages.note: Media description has rtcp-mux-only and rtcp-mux.

messages.label: Answer with port 0
messages.note: Rejects the media; the offerer disables it or re-offers without rtcp-mux-only.
